hypotheses.statement: A game with a first-time or fill-in starting quarterback (Miami with McCord, Las Vegas with Mendoza, Minnesota with Cousins) has a wider first-half-total spread than other 2026 games, so a first-half total priced from a single book's line is more uncertain, not less.
hypotheses.rule: After Sunday's games, compare the spread (sample standard deviation) of first-half totals in games with a first-time or fill-in starter against the 2026 base rate and against games with a season-long starter.
hypotheses.check_now: Descriptive only, not a test of the quarterback effect (starters per past game are U in these files): across ESPN weeks 1 to 9, first-half totals have mean 22.3 and sample standard deviation 8.8 over 136 games (E). Indianapolis and Miami games: mean 22.5, standard deviation 9.4, n = 17. Jacksonville and Tennessee games: mean 20.8, standard deviation 7.4, n = 16. The Indianapolis-Miami spread is 0.7 above the all-games spread; with n = 17 that is not a distinguishable difference.
hypotheses.falsifier: The first-time-starter games' first-half totals show a spread equal to or narrower than the base rate once enough games exist (several games, not Sunday's two or three).
hypotheses.control: Games with a season-long starter on both sides (for example Jacksonville and Tennessee so far, standard deviation 7.4, n = 16).
hypotheses.status: prospective; cannot be scored from this slate alone (n of Sunday's first-time-starter games is 2 to 3)
hypotheses.implication: If true, a one-point-off peer line is worth less than a typical single-book line. Until then it is a caution, not a finding.
